title: Modes & Permissions
description: Plan before you poke: permission modes, Shift+Tab, and allow/ask/deny rules.

theory.title: Look before you leap
theory.body:
Kip never scuttles into a new tide pool without scouting it first. **Plan mode** is Claude Code's scouting mode: Claude reads files and runs read-only commands to explore, then proposes a step-by-step plan, but it does **not** edit your source files.

Edits stay blocked until you **approve the plan**. Use it for big refactors, unfamiliar code, or any time you want to agree on the approach before a single line changes.
theory.code:
# start a session already in plan mode
claude --permission-mode plan

theory.title: Getting into plan mode
theory.body:
Mid-session, press `Shift+Tab` to cycle permission modes. The mode indicator under the prompt shows where you are: Manual (`default`), then **accept edits** (`acceptEdits`), then **plan** (`plan`).

To make a project always start in plan mode, set `defaultMode` under `permissions` in a settings file.

exercises.prompt: What does Claude do in plan mode?
options: Generates a plan and immediately applies it
Reads and explores, then proposes a plan without editing your source files
Edits files without asking but never runs commands
Runs every command without asking for permission
exercises.explanation: Plan mode is read-only exploration plus a proposed plan; edits wait for your approval.

exercises.prompt: Start a new Claude Code session directly in plan mode.
exercises.hint: The flag is --permission-mode followed by the mode name.
exercises.explanation: `--permission-mode plan` starts the session in plan mode so nothing is edited until you approve a plan.

exercises.prompt: You are mid-session and want to switch into plan mode. What do you press?
exercises.explanation: `Shift+Tab` cycles permission modes, and plan mode is one of the stops.

exercises.prompt: Match each permission mode to what it does.

pairs.right: Skips prompts; containers and VMs only

exercises.explanation: Each mode trades convenience for oversight differently, from asking every time to skipping prompts entirely.

exercises.prompt: Put a plan-mode workflow in order.
steps: Press Shift+Tab until the indicator shows plan mode
Claude explores the code and proposes a plan
Ask questions and refine the plan
Approve the plan so Claude can start editing
exercises.explanation: You agree on the approach first, and edits only begin once you approve the plan.

exercises.prompt: You are in plan mode before a risky payments refactor. Which prompt is better?
options: Explore src/payments and propose a step-by-step plan to move Stripe calls behind a PaymentProvider interface. List the files you would touch and the risks; do not edit anything yet.
exercises.explanation: The second prompt names the scope, the goal, and the expected output of the planning phase.

exercises.prompt: Make every session in this project start in plan mode.
exercises.explanation: `permissions.defaultMode` sets the mode sessions start in, and `"plan"` is plan mode.

exercises.scenario: You want to add rate limiting to the login endpoint, but you are new to this codebase. Write the prompt you would send in plan mode.
exercises.sample: Read @src/api/login.ts and the existing middleware in @src/middleware/. Propose a plan to add rate limiting to the login endpoint (5 attempts per minute per IP): which files change, whether to reuse an existing middleware pattern, how to test it, and any risks. Do not edit files yet.
exercises.explanation: A strong plan-mode prompt points at the relevant files, states the goal precisely, and asks for a plan rather than edits.

lessons.title: Auto-Accept & Cycling
lessons.description: acceptEdits, Shift+Tab and the danger zone

theory.title: Auto-accept edits
theory.body:
In `acceptEdits` mode Claude Code automatically approves **file edits** and common filesystem commands such as `mkdir`, `touch`, `mv` and `cp` inside your working directory.

Other shell commands (installing packages, pushing, publishing) still ask. It is perfect when you are iterating on code you'll review in the diff anyway.

theory.title: Cycling and the danger zone
theory.body:
`Shift+Tab` cycles Manual (`default`) → `acceptEdits` → `plan`, and, when they are available, `bypassPermissions` and `auto` as well. Watch the indicator under the prompt.

`--dangerously-skip-permissions` starts in `bypassPermissions`, which skips permission prompts. Kip only uses it inside a **container or VM** where nothing precious can be crushed.

exercises.prompt: You are in acceptEdits mode and Claude wants to run `npm publish`. What happens?
options: It runs automatically because all commands are accepted
Claude switches to plan mode first
You are still asked, since it is not a file edit or common filesystem command
exercises.explanation: acceptEdits only auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands; other shell commands still prompt.

exercises.prompt: Start a session that automatically accepts file edits.
exercises.hint: Same flag as plan mode, different value (camelCase).
exercises.explanation: `--permission-mode acceptEdits` auto-approves edits from the first turn.

exercises.prompt: You start a session with `claude --permission-mode default` and press Shift+Tab once. Which mode are you in now?
exercises.explanation: The cycle goes Manual (default) → acceptEdits → plan.

exercises.prompt: Inside a throwaway Docker container, start Claude Code so it skips permission prompts entirely.
exercises.hint: The flag name literally warns you that it is dangerous.
exercises.explanation: `--dangerously-skip-permissions` starts in bypassPermissions mode and belongs only in isolated environments.

exercises.prompt: Match each control to its job.

pairs.right: Start a session in plan mode

exercises.explanation: Keys switch modes mid-session, flags set them at launch, and /permissions manages rules.

exercises.prompt: Starting in Manual mode, walk to plan mode and then implement.
steps: Press Shift+Tab: the indicator shows accept edits
Press Shift+Tab again: the indicator shows plan mode
Ask Claude to research and propose a plan
Approve the plan and let Claude start editing
exercises.explanation: Each Shift+Tab press moves one step around the mode cycle.

exercises.prompt: You switched to acceptEdits to do a rename. Which prompt is better?
options: Rename formatDate to formatIsoDate in src/utils/date.ts, update every import, then run npm test and show me any failures.
exercises.explanation: With edits auto-approved, a precise scope and a verification step matter even more.

exercises.prompt: Where is it reasonable to use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`?
options: Anywhere, as long as you have git
Your main laptop with production credentials
A shared server everyone logs into
exercises.explanation: Skipping all prompts is only safe where Claude cannot damage anything that matters.

lessons.title: Permission Rules
lessons.description: settings.json allow, ask and deny lists

theory.title: Where rules live
theory.body:
Permission rules live in settings files:

`~/.claude/settings.json` applies to **you in every project**. `.claude/settings.json` is the **project** file you commit so the team shares it. `.claude/settings.local.json` is **personal** to this project and not committed.

Rules go in three lists under `permissions`: `allow`, `ask` and `deny`. Run `/permissions` to see every rule and which file it came from.

theory.title: Rule syntax
theory.body:
A rule is a tool name, optionally with a specifier: `Tool` or `Tool(specifier)`. Tool names include `Bash`, `Read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch`, `Glob` and `Grep`.

`Bash(npm run build)` matches that exact command. `Bash(npm run *)` matches `npm run build` and `npm run test --watch` but not `npm install`. The older `:*` suffix is equivalent: `Bash(ls:*)` = `Bash(ls *)`.

`Read(./.env)` targets a path; `WebFetch(domain:github.com)` targets a domain.

exercises.prompt: Let Claude run test scripts and read docs freely, but never read the .env file.
exercises.explanation: `allow` pre-approves matching calls and `deny` blocks them.

exercises.prompt: Match each settings file to who it applies to.
exercises.explanation: User, project and local settings let you share some rules and keep others personal.

exercises.prompt: Which rule matches `npm run build` but NOT `npm install`?
exercises.explanation: The wildcard after `npm run ` only matches commands that start with `npm run`.

exercises.prompt: Block reading .env and restrict web fetches to the Python docs.
exercises.explanation: `Read(path)` scopes file reads and `WebFetch(domain:...)` scopes fetches by domain.

exercises.prompt: Open the dialog that lists your permission rules and the file each one comes from.
exercises.hint: It is a slash command named after what it manages.
exercises.explanation: `/permissions` shows allow, ask and deny rules and lets you add or remove them.

exercises.prompt: Your team wants the same allow rules for lint and tests on every machine. Where do they go?
exercises.explanation: The project settings file is shared through version control.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to configure permissions for the repo. Which prompt is better?
options: In .claude/settings.json, add allow rules for Bash(npm run lint) and Bash(npm run test *), and a deny rule for Read(./.env). Leave other settings untouched.
exercises.explanation: Naming the file, the exact rules and the boundaries leaves no room for an overly broad allow.

exercises.scenario: Ask Claude to set up a shared permissions config: tests and lint should run without prompts, .env files must never be read, and curl should be blocked.
exercises.sample: Update @.claude/settings.json (create it if missing). Using the scripts in @package.json, add allow rules for Bash(npm run lint) and Bash(npm run test *). Add deny rules for Read(./.env), Read(./.env.*) and Bash(curl *). Do not change any other settings, and show me the final file.
exercises.explanation: Good permission prompts name exact rules and the file, so nothing broader than intended gets allowed.

theory.title: Deny first, always
theory.body:
Rules are evaluated in a fixed order: **deny**, then **ask**, then **allow**. The first match decides, and specificity does not change the order.

So a broad deny like `Bash(aws *)` blocks `aws s3 ls` even if `Bash(aws s3 ls)` is in `allow`. An allow rule can never carve an exception out of a deny rule, and a matching ask rule still prompts even if an allow rule also matches.

theory.title: Enforced, not requested
theory.body:
Permission rules are enforced **by Claude Code**, not by the model. Writing "never read .env" in `CLAUDE.md` shapes what Claude *tries*; a `deny` rule decides what is *allowed*.

A bare tool name in `deny`, like `"WebFetch"`, removes that tool from Claude's context entirely. A scoped rule like `Bash(rm *)` keeps the tool but blocks matching calls.

exercises.prompt: allow: `Bash(git *)`, deny: `Bash(git push *)`. Claude runs `git push origin main`. What happens?
options: It runs, because the allow rule is broader
It runs, because allow is listed first
exercises.explanation: Deny is checked first and the first match wins.

exercises.prompt: allow: `Bash(npm *)`, ask: `Bash(npm publish *)`. Claude runs `npm publish`. What happens?
options: Claude Code crashes on the conflict
exercises.explanation: Ask is checked before allow, so the ask rule wins.

exercises.prompt: Make `git push` always ask first, and block `rm -rf` outright.
exercises.explanation: `ask` forces a confirmation prompt and `deny` blocks the call.

exercises.prompt: Put Claude Code's rule evaluation in order.
steps: No match: fall back to the current permission mode
exercises.explanation: Deny, then ask, then allow; the first match determines the outcome.

exercises.prompt: Match each rule to its effect.
exercises.explanation: Where a rule sits (allow, ask, deny) matters as much as what it matches.

exercises.prompt: Why use a deny rule instead of writing "never read .env" in CLAUDE.md?
options: Deny rules are enforced by Claude Code; CLAUDE.md only guides the model
exercises.explanation: Instructions shape behavior, but only permission rules actually block a tool call.

exercises.prompt: Which rule matches exactly the same commands as `Bash(ls *)`?
exercises.explanation: The `:*` suffix is an equivalent way to write a trailing wildcard.

exercises.prompt: You need to guarantee Claude never reads your secrets. Which request is better?
options: Add a note to CLAUDE.md saying not to look at .env files.
Add Read(./.env) and Read(./.env.*) to the deny list in .claude/settings.json.
exercises.explanation: A deny rule is enforced every time, whereas a note is only guidance.

mission.title: Lock the Shell
mission.intro: Kip wants a safe tide pool. Set up modes and permission rules in a real repo.
checklist: Run `claude --permission-mode plan` in a real repo and ask for a plan for a small change
Press Shift+Tab a few times and watch the mode indicator change
Create `.claude/settings.json` with an allow rule for your test command and a deny rule for `Read(./.env)`
Run `/permissions` and confirm your rules appear with their source file
Ask Claude to read `.env` and watch the deny rule block it
mission.explanation: You now plan before editing and let enforced rules, not hope, guard your secrets.

cheatsheet.description: Cycle permission modes: Manual, accept edits, plan, and more.
Start a session in read-only plan mode.
Mode that auto-approves file edits and common filesystem commands.

Project settings, committed and shared with the team.

Rule matching any command starting with npm run.
